result:
There is a particular kind of quiet in old maps. Not the silence of an empty room, but the hush of places someone drew from memory, guessed at, or simply left blank. I find myself drawn to the margins, where cartographers wrote things like *here be dragons* or *unexplored* or nothing at all. Those blank spaces feel more honest than the crisp grids of modern navigation, which promise that every inch has been measured and known.

I like thinking about the people who made those early maps. They walked or sailed toward edges they could not see, and they drew what they believed was there. Some were right, some wildly wrong, and some drew islands that existed only because a sailor's tired eyes saw a smudge of cloud on the horizon. Their mistakes are part of the record now, almost as valuable as their discoveries.

Maybe that's why I think of maps as a kind of conversation between the known and the unknown. Every line is a claim, and every blank is an admission. A good map knows where its knowledge ends.

There is something to learn from that in ordinary life, too. Most of us carry small maps of our own: beliefs about how the world works, about other people, about ourselves. We fill in the edges with confident ink even when we have never actually been there. It would be healthier, I think, to leave a few more spaces blank, to write in pencil, and to occasionally redraw the coastline when new evidence washes ashore.

Then again, I may be romanticizing it. A blank space on a map can also mean a place where people were simply never sent, or where nobody bothered to ask. The poetry of the unknown is easier to admire from a comfortable chair than from the deck of a leaky ship.

Still, I keep coming back to the image of a hand bent over parchment, deciding what to draw next. Uncertain, careful, hopeful. It seems like a decent way to approach almost anything.
